passages.original: Duae maxime et in hac re dissident sectae, Epicureorum et Stoicorum, sed utraque ad otium diversa via mittit. Epicurus ait : " Non accedet ad rem publicam sapiens, nisi si quid intervenerit "; Zenon ait : " Accedet ad rem publicam, nisi si quid impedient."
passages.english: Two sects in particular disagree on this matter too, the Epicureans and the Stoics, but each of them sends [one] to leisure by a different road. Epicurus says: "The wise man will not take part in public affairs, unless something intervenes"; Zeno says: "He will take part in public affairs, unless something prevents him."
passages.notes: "impedient" is evidently an error for "impedierit" ("prevents"); translated accordingly.

passages.original: ita et haec ipsa voluptaria secta in actu est. Quidni in actu sit ? cum ipse dicat Epicurus aliquando se recessurum a voluptate, dolorem etiam adpetiturum, si aut voluptati imminebit paenitentia aut dolor minor pro graviore sumetur ? Quo pertinet haec dicere ?
passages.english: so even this very sect devoted to pleasure is engaged in action. Why should it not be engaged in action, when Epicurus himself says that he will at times withdraw from pleasure, and even seek out pain, if either regret threatens to follow pleasure or a lesser pain is taken on in place of a heavier one? What is the point of saying these things?
